raw_text: {"schema_version":"chat_response_v1","response_type":"answer","answer_text":"At constant pressure, the volume of a given gas sample is directly proportional to its absolute temperature, which is Charles's law [ev_006]. The source states that volume increases as temperature increases and decreases as temperature decreases at constant pressure [ev_003]. Because V/T is constant at constant pressure and amount [ev_004], V2 = V1 × T2/T1. With your values, V2 = 0.450 L × (400 K / 300 K) = 0.600 L; the kelvin units cancel, leaving liters. The expected final volume is therefore 0.600 L [ev_004]. The temperature must be on the kelvin scale because the ideal gas law defines T as temperature on the kelvin scale [ev_004], and absolute zero is the temperature at which a gas volume would be zero according to Charles's law [ev_010]. Ratios of Celsius values would not be proportional to absolute temperature, so the kelvin scale is required [ev_006][ev_010]. No, these temperatures alone would not determine the final volume if pressure were also allowed to change. The ideal gas law relates P, V, n and T, and specifying any four of these terms, together with R, permits calculation of the fifth [ev_002][ev_004].
